source_text: I. Cum esset persecutio sub Diocletiano et Maximiano imperatoribus, quando diversis agonibus concertantes Christiani, a tyrannis illata supplicia devota deo mente suscipientes, praemiis se perpetuis participes efficiebant. quod et factum est circa famulum dei Irenaeum episcopum urbis Sirmiensium, cuius iam nunc vobis certamen pandam victoriamque ostendam; qui pro modestia sua ingenita et timore divino, cui operibus rectis inserviebat, dignus nominis sui inventus est. II. Comprehensus itaque oblatus est Probo praesidi Pannoniae. Probus praeses dixit ad eum: Obtemperans praeceptis divinis sacrifica diis. Irenaeus episcopus respondit: Qui diis et non deo sacrificat eradicabitur. Probus praeses dixit: Clementissimi principes iusserunt aut sacrificare, aut tormentis succumbere debere. Irenaeus respondit: Mihi praeceptum est tormenta magis suscipere quam deum denegans daemoniis sacrificare. Probus praeses dixit: Aut sacrifica, aut faciam te torqueri. Irenaeus respondit: Gaudeo si feceris, ut domini mei passionibus particeps inveniar. Probus praeses iussit [eam — for eum?] vexari. cumque acerbissime vexaretur, dixit ad eum praeses: Quid dicis, Irenaee? sacrifica. Irenaeus respondit: Sacrifico per bonam confessionem deo meo, cui semper sacrificavi.
pass_a_gloss: With persecution existing under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, when Christians struggling in various contests were receiving punishments inflicted by tyrants with mind devoted to God and were making themselves sharers in everlasting rewards, this also happened concerning Irenaeus, bishop of Sirmium, whose contest I will now lay open and whose victory I will show, who was found worthy of his name because of inborn modesty and divine fear, which he served by right works; arrested, he was brought to Probus the governor of Pannonia, who ordered him to obey and sacrifice, and Irenaeus answered he must suffer torments rather than deny God, rejoiced to share his Lord's sufferings, was harshly tortured, and said he sacrifices by good confession to his God.
pass_b_english: There was a persecution under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, when Christians contending in many arenas of trial received the punishments inflicted by tyrants with a mind devoted to God, and so made themselves sharers in everlasting rewards.

This also came to pass in the case of Irenaeus, servant of God and bishop of the city of Sirmium, whose contest I will now lay open before you and whose victory I will show, who for his inborn modesty and godly fear, which he served by upright deeds, was found worthy of his name.
He was arrested and brought before Probus, the governor of Pannonia.
Governor Probus said to him: Obey the divine commands and sacrifice to the gods.
Bishop Irenaeus answered: Whoever sacrifices to gods and not to God shall be rooted out (Exodus 22:20).
Governor Probus said: The most merciful emperors have commanded that you must either sacrifice or fall under tortures.
Irenaeus answered: I have been commanded rather to endure torments than to deny God and sacrifice to demons.
Governor Probus said: Either sacrifice, or I will have you tortured.
Irenaeus answered: I shall rejoice if you do it, so that I may be found a sharer in the sufferings of my Lord.
Governor Probus ordered him to be tormented.
And when he was being tormented most bitterly, the governor said to him: What do you say, Irenaeus?
Irenaeus answered: I sacrifice through a faithful confession to my God, to whom I have always sacrificed.

choices.english: contending in many arenas of trial
choices.why: ablative of circumstance with present participle; agon here is athletic-martyr contest imagery, not a single agony
ablative of manner modifying suscipientes; deo is dative of devotion, not ablative of agent
rejected: by a mind devoted by God

choices.why: per plus accusative gives means; in martyr context confessio is public witness, not private admission
